title: The Bank Transfer That Hangs
scenario: A payments service moves money with `transfer(from, to, amount)`. Each account has its own mutex. The function locks `from`, then locks `to`, moves the money, and unlocks both. Under load the service occasionally freezes completely: CPU drops to zero, and thread dumps show two worker threads, one inside `transfer(alice, bob, …)` and one inside `transfer(bob, alice, …)`, each blocked on its second lock.
question: What is the most robust fix?

options.text: Always acquire the two account locks in a global order, e.g. lower account ID first, regardless of transfer direction.
options.explanation: The hang is a circular wait: T1 holds alice and wants bob, T2 holds bob and wants alice. If every thread takes locks in the same global order, a cycle is impossible: whoever gets the lower-ID lock first will also get the higher one. This removes one of the four Coffman conditions (circular wait) with almost no runtime cost.

options.text: Replace the mutexes with recursive (re-entrant) mutexes.
options.explanation: Recursive mutexes only let the *same* thread re-acquire a lock it already holds. Here two *different* threads each hold the lock the other needs, so re-entrancy changes nothing.

options.text: When the second lock isn't available, release the first, sleep a random few milliseconds, and retry.
options.explanation: This avoids permanent deadlock (it breaks hold-and-wait), but it can livelock (both threads keep backing off together), adds latency, and wastes work under contention. It's a fallback for when you *can't* impose an order, not the robust first fix.

options.text: Give worker threads a higher scheduling priority so they finish transfers faster.
options.explanation: Both threads are blocked, not slow. Priority affects who runs when there's CPU contention, and a blocked thread doesn't run at all. The cycle stays.

key_takeaway: Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait. Imposing a global lock order is the cheapest way to make circular wait impossible.
common_misconception: "Deadlocks are timing bugs, so making the code faster or adding retries fixes them." Speed only changes how often the bad interleaving happens. The fix is structural: make the cycle impossible.
